positioning: A brick wrapped in silk. A glossy, golden-eyed cat that adores its people.
story: The modern Burmese traces to a single cat. In the 1930s a small brown cat named Wong Mau was brought from Burma to the United States, and a careful breeding program built an entire breed around her warm sable coat and sweet nature.

It is deceptively solid. The Burmese looks compact and rounded but feels surprisingly heavy in the hand, leading to the old description of a brick wrapped in silk. The short, glossy coat lies close to a muscular body, set off by large, round, golden-yellow eyes.

The temperament is its glory. Burmese are devoted, people-oriented, and endlessly affectionate, often called the most dog-like of cats for the way they follow, greet, and insist on laps. They stay playful and kittenish well into adulthood.
They do not like to be alone and thrive in busy, loving homes. The breed also helped create the Tonkinese through crosses with the Siamese, and it comes in sable and several diluted shades.

A Burmese is famously people-dependent. It wants laps, shoulders, and conversation, follows its owners from room to room, and stays playful and kitten-like for years, which makes it a delightful companion and a poor choice for anyone away from home all day.

The short, satiny coat needs only a weekly wipe, but the breed carries a few risks worth knowing, including dental disease, diabetes, and, in some lines, a serious skull deformity and a condition that causes painful sensitivity, so reputable breeders test carefully.

Nearly the entire breed descends from Wong Mau, bred to fix her warm brown coat and sweet temperament.
Affectionate and people-focused, it wants company and laps and dislikes being left alone for long.
A short, satiny, close-lying coat, classically warm sable brown, also in dilute shades, with golden eyes.
A parent of the Tonkinese through crosses with the Siamese, and a long-standing favorite for its dog-like devotion.
Give it laps, play, and company. The Burmese is devoted and social and unhappy left alone for long stretches.
Easy to groom, but watch for dental disease and diabetes and choose breeders who screen for known inherited conditions.

last_walk:
The lamp is on, and the snow keeps falling.
The Burmese has followed you from room to room all week. It has sat on your book, your sweater, and your plans. Now it curls into the quilt with a sigh, content to be exactly where you are. A heavy little heart, warm all the way through.
